title: Running Scripts from Repository Files
learning_outcomes: Explain the key behavior of running scripts from repository files and identify when it should be used.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on running scripts from repository files. content_blocks.code:
name: Run a repository script
on: workflow_dispatch
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  validate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Run validation script
        run: python scripts/validate.py
content_blocks.expected_output: The runner checks out the repository and runs `scripts/validate.py`; it succeeds only when the script exits with status zero.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Use a script that actually exists in the repository and ensure required runtimes/dependencies are installed first.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Remove or revert the workflow after validating the repository script.

content_blocks.title: Practice and verification

items.title: Syntax and scope
items.text: Check YAML indentation and confirm whether the setting belongs at workflow, job, or step level.

items.title: Permissions and trust
items.text: Start with read-only access. If the example needs more access, explain the exact operation and reduce permissions again afterwards.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Use the run summary and first failing step. A green result is meaningful only when the intended checks actually ran.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain running scripts from repository files, read the example, and identify a way to validate it. The wider system goal remains: Decide when to run a shell command, invoke an action, or move logic into a repository script.

content.expected_output: The expected result is the behavior described here: Committed scripts keep complex automation testable and reviewable; invoke them with explicit arguments, handle exit codes, and set executable permissions where needed. The real result depends on the repository, selected ref, configured permissions, and runner availability.
troubleshooting: If a workflow never starts, verify the workflow is under `.github/workflows/`, the event and filters match, and repository/organization Actions policy allows it.
If a step fails, inspect the first failed step, exit code, stderr, installed tool versions, permissions, and runner/network state before retrying.
If a job is skipped or data is missing, inspect `if`, `needs`, outputs, artifact names/paths, and cache keys; jobs do not automatically share filesystems.
common_mistakes: Assuming YAML parsing proves the workflow runs correctly or matches the intended trigger.
Granting broad token permissions, printing environment values, or exposing a secret to untrusted code.
Using a placeholder command as evidence of a real build, test, deployment, or security scan.
